claim: NCERT Grade 9 defines taxes as compulsory payments by individuals and businesses to the government, used to fund public services such as schools, hospitals, transport and defence
value: tax = compulsory payment to fund public services
source: NCERT Grade 9 Economics (iest2), Ch5 Managing Your Personal Finances; First Edition
second_source: IGNOU (eGyankosh), Unit 13 Sources of Revenue: Tax and Non-tax [Section 13.2 (compulsory contribution imposed by a public authority, not a penalty)]

claim: NCERT Grade 9 splits taxes into direct (paid directly on a person's or organisation's income or profits, e.g. income tax) and indirect (added to the price of goods and services, e.g. GST)
value: direct = on income; indirect = added to price
source: NCERT Grade 9 Economics (iest2), Ch5 Managing Your Personal Finances; First Edition
second_source: IGNOU (eGyankosh), Unit 10 Direct and Indirect Taxation [Unit 10 section 10.2, p.156]

claim: IGNOU: a tax is direct when its impact and its incidence fall on the same tax unit; for an indirect tax they fall on different units. How easily the burden can be shifted depends on the elasticity of demand and supply of the taxed commodity, and in reality the line between direct and indirect blurs
value: impact vs incidence; shifting depends on elasticity
source: IGNOU (eGyankosh), Unit 10 Direct and Indirect Taxation
second_source: IGNOU (eGyankosh), Unit 13 Sources of Revenue: Tax and Non-tax [Section 13.2: indirect tax is paid partly or wholly by others; direct tax incidence cannot be shifted]
note: Source gives no date. Use as the concept source for 'who really pays'. 'Impact' = who first pays the government; 'incidence' = who finally bears it (IGNOU wording, our paraphrase).

claim: IGNOU shows with a supply-demand diagram that when a tax raises a commodity's price, the whole increase need not be passed on to the buyer, so demand falls less and the price rises less than the full tax; the split of the burden depends on the price elasticities
value: tax burden is shared between buyer and seller
source: IGNOU (eGyankosh), Unit 10 Direct and Indirect Taxation
note: Basis for the 'guess first' idea: a Rs 100 tax on a good does not always raise the shelf price by Rs 100. The diagram itself is IGNOU's; we draw our own.

claim: The CGST Act makes the supplier (the 'taxable person') the legal payer: central tax on intra-State supplies 'shall be paid by the taxable person'
source: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, as amended up to 01.01.2022 (CBIC)
second_source: CBEC/CBIC, Frequently Asked Questions on Goods and Services Tax, 2nd edition, 31 Mar 2017 [Q1: burden of tax is to be borne by the final consumer]

claim: CBIC's own FAQ describes GST as a destination-based tax on consumption, levied at every stage with credit for earlier-stage tax, so only value addition is taxed and the burden is borne by the final consumer
source: CBEC/CBIC, Frequently Asked Questions on Goods and Services Tax, 2nd edition, 31 Mar 2017
second_source: NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics (leec1), Ch5 Government Budget and the Economy; page footers Reprint 2026-27 [Box 5.3, printed p.82]
note: Legal payer (A05) and who bears it (A06) differ. The final consumer's burden depends on the price the seller can charge: that is A03/A04 (our inference, not stated by CBIC).

claim: NCERT Class XII divides tax revenue into direct taxes (personal income tax, corporation tax) and indirect taxes (excise, customs, service tax), and says wealth tax, gift tax and estate duty never raised much, calling them 'paper taxes'
value: direct: income tax, corporation tax; indirect: excise, customs, service tax
source: NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics (leec1), Ch5 Government Budget and the Economy; page footers Reprint 2026-27

source: NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics (leec1), Ch5 Government Budget and the Economy; page footers Reprint 2026-27

source: IGNOU (eGyankosh), Block 7 Fiscal and Monetary Policy, Unit 22 section 22.5

second_source: IGNOU (eGyankosh), Unit 10 Direct and Indirect Taxation [Section 10.2.1, printed p.157 (progressive, proportional); its regressive sentence is garbled]

[Audit 11 Nov 2026] Page cite corrected: section 22.5 starts on printed p.365 (PDF p.25 of block7.pdf); definitions A-C are on printed pp.365-366. The earlier "p.~342+" was wrong. claim: NCERT Class XII says indirect taxes 'are regressive in nature' because they 'impact all income groups equally'. IGNOU also calls indirect taxes regressive and likely to increase inequality (Unit 10 p.156) and, for excise on goods such as petroleum products, gives a different reason: both poor and rich use them, so the poor pay a higher percentage of their income as tax (Unit 10 p.161). That share-of-income reason is not the same as 'impact equally'
value: indirect taxes tend to be regressive
source: NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics (leec1), Ch5 Government Budget and the Economy; page footers Reprint 2026-27
second_source: IGNOU (eGyankosh), Unit 10 Direct and Indirect Taxation [Section 10.2, p.156 (indirect taxes are regressive, may increase inequalities); excise discussion, p.161 (poor pay a higher percentage of income)]
note: NCERT's reason is loose: equal rupee burden is not equal burden as a share of income. Teach 'tend to be regressive' with the share-of-income reason (our inference). A spot-the-mistake question. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Claim re-worded: the share-of-income reason is IGNOU's own (Unit 10 p.161, on excise on goods such as petroleum products), not an unsourced 'standard reason'. Both sides are read correctly: NCERT p.80 ('impact all income groups equally'), IGNOU p.156 (regressive, may increase inequalities). Teach 'tend to be regressive' with the share-of-income reason.

claim: Article 269A: GST on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce (imports count as inter-State) is levied and collected by the Government of India and apportioned between the Union and the States as Parliament provides by law on the Council's recommendation; the amount apportioned to a State is not part of the Consolidated Fund of India
source: Constitution of India, as on 1 May 2024 (Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice; file hosted at cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in)

source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II Sec 1, 8 Sep 2016 (Legislative Department)

source: Constitution of India, as on 1 May 2024 (Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice; file hosted at cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in)

claim: Every decision of the GST Council needs a majority of at least three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting; the Centre's vote carries one-third of the total votes cast and all the States together carry two-thirds; quorum is one-half of the members
source: Constitution of India, as on 1 May 2024 (Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice; file hosted at cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in)
second_source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II Sec 1, 8 Sep 2016 (Legislative Department) [Section 12]
note: Our arithmetic from the article: the Centre's one-third is more than the one-quarter that can stop a three-fourths vote, so the Centre can block any decision; all States together hold two-thirds, below three-fourths, so they cannot pass a decision without the Centre. The votes count only those 'present and voting'. This is our reading; show only the fractions on screen.

claim: Union of India v Mohit Minerals (19 May 2022): the Supreme Court held that GST Council recommendations are not binding on the Union and the States; they have persuasive value
source: Supreme Court of India, Union of India v. M/s Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022 and connected appeals, judgment of 19 May 2022 (D.Y. Chandrachud, Surya Kant, Vikram Nath JJ.)
note: Three-judge bench; single judgment (Chandrachud J. signs with Surya Kant and Vikram Nath JJ.).

claim: Reasons the Court gave: Parliament's amendment history (the omission of a proposed Article 279B authority) shows recommendations were meant to be only persuasive; Article 279A has no non-obstante clause; Article 246A is not made subject to Article 279A; Parliament and State legislatures have simultaneous power on GST; the recommendations come from collaborative dialogue, and treating them as binding edicts would disrupt fiscal federalism
source: Supreme Court of India, Union of India v. M/s Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022 and connected appeals, judgment of 19 May 2022 (D.Y. Chandrachud, Surya Kant, Vikram Nath JJ.)
note: The judgment's own wording of the first reason refers to 'Article 279B' and 'Article 279(1)'; quote cautiously. Reasons are the Court's (the majority/single judgment), not our summary of the debate.

claim: The Court also said that when the Government makes rules under the CGST and IGST Acts it is bound by the Council's recommendations, but that does not make every recommendation binding on the legislatures' power to enact primary legislation
source: Supreme Court of India, Union of India v. M/s Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022 and connected appeals, judgment of 19 May 2022 (D.Y. Chandrachud, Surya Kant, Vikram Nath JJ.)

claim: The Union argued that Council recommendations should be binding on Parliament and State legislatures, because if they are not binding there would be an impasse in which different Central and State laws could guide the same field; the Court did not accept this
source: Supreme Court of India, Union of India v. M/s Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022 and connected appeals, judgment of 19 May 2022 (D.Y. Chandrachud, Surya Kant, Vikram Nath JJ.)
page_or_section: Part C paras 45-46, printed pp.77-78 (Union contention also para 21, printed p.54); Court conclusion para 148(i), printed pp.150-151
note: A party's submission, not a holding. Page of the Union's argument not isolated; the sentence sits in the Part K discussion of the cooperative federalism question. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Claim re-worded to the Court's own record: the Union argued that if recommendations are not binding it would lead to an impasse where different Central and State laws could guide the same field (paras 45-46, printed pp.77-78); the opening contention that recommendations bind the legislature and executive is para 21 (printed p.54). 'Disorder' was our word, not the Court's. Court's answer: para 148(i), printed pp.150-151.

claim: The Court described Indian federalism in GST as a dialogue running between cooperative and 'uncooperative' federalism, in which the Union and the States may use means from collaboration to contestation, and said States and Union have equal power to legislate on GST
source: Supreme Court of India, Union of India v. M/s Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022 and connected appeals, judgment of 19 May 2022 (D.Y. Chandrachud, Surya Kant, Vikram Nath JJ.)
note: The 2023 GS II Q15 phrase 'accommodative federalism' is not the Court's term; the judgment uses cooperative and collaborative federalism (open item).

claim: The case itself was about IGST on ocean freight: the Court held that charging Indian importers IGST on the shipping line's service in CIF contracts, by notification under the IGST Act, was invalid (it conflicted with the composite-supply rule and created a deeming fiction by delegated legislation), and dismissed the appeals
value: IGST on ocean freight struck down
source: Supreme Court of India, Union of India v. M/s Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022 and connected appeals, judgment of 19 May 2022 (D.Y. Chandrachud, Surya Kant, Vikram Nath JJ.)

claim: The Government's own description: the Council is a constitutional body that brings the Centre and the States together in decisions, and GSTN, the IT company that runs the common GST portal, is owned 50% by the Centre and 50% by the States
value: Council = cooperative federalism (Govt's own words); GSTN 50:50
source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Nine Years of GST: Simplifying Taxation, Strengthening India', 30 Jun 2026
note: This is the Ministry of Finance's characterisation, not an independent finding.

claim: NCERT Class XII Box 5.3: GST is the single comprehensive indirect tax, operational from 1 July 2017, on supply of goods and services from manufacturer or service provider to consumer; it is a destination-based consumption tax with input tax credit
value: GST = destination-based consumption tax with ITC
source: NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics (leec1), Ch5 Government Budget and the Economy; page footers Reprint 2026-27
second_source: CBEC/CBIC, Frequently Asked Questions on Goods and Services Tax, 2nd edition, 31 Mar 2017 [Q1 and Q2 (destination principle)]

claim: NCERT Class XII: before GST, tax was imposed on the total value of the commodity with minimal input credit, so the tax on inputs was taxed again; this is cascading. Under GST the tax is paid at every stage with credit for the previous stage's tax, so it is effectively a tax on value addition
source: NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics (leec1), Ch5 Government Budget and the Economy; page footers Reprint 2026-27
second_source: GST Council / CBIC Directorate General of Taxpayer Services, flyer 'Input Tax Credit Mechanism', 2019 [Page 1 (cascading explained)]

claim: GST Council flyer worked example: a pen maker's inputs cost Rs 10 and carried Rs 1 of excise; the pen sold at Rs 20 carried Rs 2 of excise (credit of Rs 1 used), so the price became Rs 22; the VAT that followed was charged on all Rs 22, including the Rs 2 excise, which is 'tax on tax'
value: Rs 10 inputs + Re 1 excise; pen Rs 20 + Rs 2 = Rs 22; VAT on Rs 22
source: GST Council / CBIC Directorate General of Taxpayer Services, flyer 'Input Tax Credit Mechanism', 2019
note: Best everyday story for cascading. Excise and VAT were separate taxes with no credit between them; that is the gap GST closed. The flyer does not give the VAT rate, so no rupee VAT figure.

claim: GST is dual: the Centre levies CGST and the State levies SGST on supplies within a State (UTGST in Union territories without legislature); IGST is levied by the Centre on inter-State supplies and imports, and shared; IGST rates are generally twice the CGST or SGST rate
source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Nine Years of GST: Simplifying Taxation, Strengthening India', 30 Jun 2026
second_source: GST Council / CBIC Directorate General of Taxpayer Services, flyer 'Input Tax Credit Mechanism', 2019 [Page 1 list (a)-(d)]

claim: Credit of CGST is used first against CGST, then IGST; credit of SGST/UTGST first against SGST/UTGST, then IGST; credit of IGST first against IGST, then CGST, then SGST/UTGST. Under s.49A/49B, IGST credit must be used up first, and SGST/UTGST credit may pay IGST only where the CGST credit balance is not available
source: GST Council / CBIC Directorate General of Taxpayer Services, flyer 'Input Tax Credit Mechanism', 2019
page_or_section: Table of utilisation (flyer); CGST Act s.49(5), 49A, 49B

[Audit 11 Nov 2026] Claim completed: the flyer table is a simplification. Checked against CGST Act s.49(5), s.49A and s.49B (as on 1.1.2022): IGST credit must be used up first; CGST/SGST credit may pay IGST only after that; SGST/UTGST credit may pay IGST only where the CGST credit balance is not available. claim: Under section 9(1) of the CGST Act, central tax is levied on all intra-State supplies of goods or services, except alcoholic liquor for human consumption, at rates not exceeding 20 per cent notified on the Council's recommendation

note: With the equal SGST ceiling in the State Acts (not read) the legal ceiling is 40% on an intra-State supply; the IGST Act ceiling was not read (open item).

claim: GST covers almost all goods and services; alcoholic liquor for human consumption is outside it by the Constitution's own definition; electricity is outside; five petroleum products (crude, petrol, diesel, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel) are outside until the Council fixes a date

source: CBEC/CBIC, Frequently Asked Questions on Goods and Services Tax, 2nd edition, 31 Mar 2017

claim: GST taxpayers rose from 66.5 lakh in 2017 to 1.65 crore in May 2026; the goods registration threshold went from Rs 20 lakh to Rs 40 lakh (April 2019) and the composition limit from Rs 75 lakh to Rs 1.5 crore (other than some special category States)

Figures 66.5 lakh, 1.65 crore, Rs 20 to 40 lakh (Apr 2019) and Rs 75 lakh to 1.5 crore re-read in the Nine Years backgrounder.

claim: Under the destination principle, GST revenue accrues to the authority with jurisdiction over the place of consumption (CBIC FAQ Q2); CBIC's About GST page gives the example that goods moved from Tamil Nadu to Kerala bear IGST, whose revenue is shared between the Centre and the States

note: [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Attribution corrected: the Tamil Nadu to Kerala example is on the CBIC About GST page (What is IGST?), not in FAQ Q2; FAQ Q2 carries only the destination principle.

claim: CBIC expected GST to cut cascading, build a common national market, make products competitive, and reduce the overall burden on goods, which it estimated at 25%-30%, for consumers
source: CBEC/CBIC, Frequently Asked Questions on Goods and Services Tax, 2nd edition, 31 Mar 2017
second_source: NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics (leec1), Ch5 Government Budget and the Economy; page footers Reprint 2026-27 [Box 5.3, printed p.83 (higher growth expected, GDP up about 2%)]

claim: CBIC lists the State taxes GST replaced: State VAT, Central Sales Tax, luxury tax, entry tax (all forms), entertainment and amusement tax (except where levied by local bodies), taxes on advertisements, purchase tax, taxes on lotteries, betting and gambling, and State surcharges and cesses relating to goods and services

source: CBEC/CBIC, Frequently Asked Questions on Goods and Services Tax, 2nd edition, 31 Mar 2017

The Compensation Act settles it: it lists entry tax, octroi and local body tax levied under the old State List entry 52 as taxes subsumed into GST

second_source: CBIC, About GST: 'GST - Concept & Status (05-04-2017)' web page [Subsumed-taxes list vs FAQ Q3 vs ITC flyer]

claim: The Ministry of Finance says GST subsumed 17 different taxes and 13 cesses into one framework
source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Nine Years of GST: Simplifying Taxation, Strengthening India', 30 Jun 2026
page_or_section: Opening section 'GST: A Milestone in India's Tax Reform Journey'
note: Only one publisher for the count. The CBIC lists above name fewer separate items because they group some (VAT, cesses). Do not itemise to 17 + 13 on screen.

claim: Customs duty is still collected separately: the 2026-27 Budget estimates customs revenue of Rs 2,71,200 crore and Union excise duties of Rs 3,88,910 crore (excise survives on the products the Constitution leaves with the Union)
source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Budget at a Glance 2026-27, Feb 2026
second_source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II Sec 1, 8 Sep 2016 (Legislative Department) [Section 17: Union List entry 84 now covers only the five petroleum goods and tobacco]

claim: Gross GST collection (CGST+SGST+IGST, without compensation cess for 2025-26) was around Rs 7.4 lakh crore in 2017-18, Rs 13.76 lakh crore in 2021-22 and Rs 22.27 lakh crore in 2025-26, and about Rs 4.37 lakh crore in April-May 2026
source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Nine Years of GST: Simplifying Taxation, Strengthening India', 30 Jun 2026
note: 2017-18 covers July 2017 to March 2018 only (nine months; our reading, since GST began 1 Jul 2017). 'Gross' is not defined in the release. Monthly PIB releases and the GST Council data were not read, so year-by-year figures between these are NOT FOUND here (open item). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Cess status checked at the GST portal (Monthly GST data, 31/03/2026, Total Gross GST Revenue): 2025-26 = Rs 22,27,096 crore, CGST+SGST+IGST WITHOUT compensation cess (cess shown separately; net cess 99,039 crore). So 22.27 is ex-cess. Not like-for-like with the Rs 22.08 lakh crore for 2024-25 in PIB 4 Sep 2025, which appears to include cess (portal 2024-25 ex-cess is Rs 20,55,515 crore; gap about 1.5 lakh crore matches the cess line, our inference). 7.4 (2017-18) and 13.76 (2021-22) not checked at the portal.

claim: The 'GST' line in the Union Budget is only the Centre's part: Budget 2026-27 shows GST (CGST) at Rs 10,19,020 crore against gross tax revenue of Rs 44,04,086 crore, i.e. 23.1% (our arithmetic); the gross GST collection of Rs 22.27 lakh crore in 2025-26 includes the States' SGST
value: Budget 'GST' 10,19,020 crore vs gross collection 22.27 lakh crore
source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Budget at a Glance 2026-27, Feb 2026
second_source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Receipt Budget 2026-2027, Feb 2026 [explanation of item 8 (GST): 'Budget Estimate for FY 2026-27 of CGST is Rs 10,19,020 crore']
note: Common confusion: the two numbers measure different things. Whether Budget 'GST' for earlier years also carries IGST settlements and compensation cess: 2025-26 RE shows compensation cess of Rs 88,000 crore inside the GST line; 2026-27 shows none. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Receipt Budget cite corrected: the CGST sentence is in the explanation of item 8 (GST), next to item 9.03, not 'section 9'. Re-read: Budget at a Glance GST line 10,19,020 and gross tax revenue 44,04,086 (23.1%); 22.27 lakh crore gross is without cess (see F06). 2025-26 RE GST line 10,46,480 includes compensation cess 88,000.

claim: Budget 2026-27 share of gross tax revenue (our arithmetic from the Budget at a Glance table): direct taxes (corporation tax Rs 12,31,000 crore + taxes on income Rs 14,66,000 crore) = 61.2%; GST, customs and Union excise (Rs 10,19,020 + 2,71,200 + 3,88,910 crore) = 38.1%
value: direct 61.2% vs GST+customs+excise 38.1% of gross tax revenue
source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Budget at a Glance 2026-27, Feb 2026
note: Percentages are ours; the Budget does not label 'direct' and 'indirect'. Gross tax revenue is before States' share. Other taxes (Rs 17,700 crore) and UT taxes left out. Consistent with NCERT's remark that the government relies more on direct taxes (B06/A10).

claim: Of each rupee the Union government receives in 2026-27, GST and other taxes supply 15 paise; income tax 21 paise; corporation tax 18 paise; Union excise 6 paise; customs 4 paise; borrowings and other liabilities 24 paise
value: GST & other taxes 15 paise of the rupee
source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Budget at a Glance 2026-27, Feb 2026
page_or_section: Rupee Comes From chart, PDF p.6
note: Shares are net of the States' share of taxes and duties (chart note 1). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Note corrected: the chart's note 1 says total receipts INCLUDE the States' share of taxes and duties (netted in the table on page 1), so the paise shares are of gross receipts (about Rs 68,73,570 crore), not net of States' share. Check: borrowings 16,63,066 / 68,73,570 = 24%, corporation tax 18%, income tax 21%, GST 15%, excise 6%, customs 4%. Shares on printed p.2.

claim: The States' share of the Union's net tax proceeds: the 16th Finance Commission recommended keeping it at 41% and the Government accepted; the Budget 2026-27 deducts Rs 15,26,255 crore as States' share from gross tax revenue
source: Ministry of Finance: Explanatory Memorandum as to the Action Taken on the Recommendations of the Sixteenth Finance Commission, Feb 2026
second_source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Budget at a Glance 2026-27, Feb 2026 [Receipts table, PDF p.10 (Less - State's share)]
note: Period covered by the award is not stated in the Explanatory Memorandum text read; do not state years. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Note corrected: the Explanatory Memorandum para 2 does state that the Report covers 2026-27 to 2030-31 (from 1 April 2026), so the period can be stated. 41% is of the net proceeds (divisible pool), not of gross tax revenue; Rs 15,26,255 crore is the Budget's deduction, not 41% of the gross.

claim: Why compensation: the Compensation Act exists to compensate the States for loss of revenue from implementing GST, as the 101st Act required for five years; States had given up their power to tax sales independently
source: The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 (No. 15 of 2017), Gazette of India Extraordinary 12 Apr 2017 (copy on gstcouncil.gov.in)
second_source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II Sec 1, 8 Sep 2016 (Legislative Department) [Section 18]
note: 'States gave up taxing power' is our reading of Art 246A/entry changes (C03, C14).

claim: The projected nominal growth rate of revenue subsumed for a State is 14% per year during the transition period
source: The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 (No. 15 of 2017), Gazette of India Extraordinary 12 Apr 2017 (copy on gstcouncil.gov.in)

claim: The base year is the financial year ending 31 March 2016 (2015-16); base-year revenue is what the State and its local bodies collected that year, net of refunds, from the taxes subsumed into GST (VAT, CST, entry tax/octroi, luxury and entertainment taxes, advertisement tax, etc.), as audited by the CAG; taxes on petroleum goods and alcohol are left out
source: The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 (No. 15 of 2017), Gazette of India Extraordinary 12 Apr 2017 (copy on gstcouncil.gov.in)

claim: Compensation for a State = projected revenue minus actual revenue: projected revenue is the base-year revenue grown at 14% a year (the Act's example: 100 x (1.14)^3 for 2018-19); actual revenue = State GST collected net of refunds + IGST apportioned to the State + other related taxes; computed and released every two months provisionally and finally after CAG-audited figures
source: The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 (No. 15 of 2017), Gazette of India Extraordinary 12 Apr 2017 (copy on gstcouncil.gov.in)
second_source: Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance: 'GST Compensation Options' paper, annexed to PIB release of 29 Aug 2020 [Background section: 'projected revenue (at a compound growth rate of 14% ...) minus the actual revenue']

claim: The transition period is five years from the date a State's GST Act came into force; the cess may be levied for five years 'or for such period as may be prescribed' on the Council's recommendation
value: 5-year transition; cess period can be set
source: The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 (No. 15 of 2017), Gazette of India Extraordinary 12 Apr 2017 (copy on gstcouncil.gov.in)
second_source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Payment of GST compensation to States in times of COVID-19 pandemic' (Rajya Sabha written reply), 7 Dec 2021 [Para: compensation 'for a period of five years from the date of implementation of GST']
note: GST began 1 Jul 2017; five years therefore ended 30 Jun 2022 (our arithmetic; the Act ties the period to each State's own start date).

claim: The compensation cess is levied on notified goods in the Act's Schedule up to the stated caps; its proceeds go to a non-lapsable GST Compensation Fund in the Public Account of India, and all compensation is paid out of that Fund. At the end of the transition period, any unspent balance is split 50:50 between the Centre and the States
source: The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 (No. 15 of 2017), Gazette of India Extraordinary 12 Apr 2017 (copy on gstcouncil.gov.in)
second_source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Budget at a Glance 2026-27, Feb 2026 [Footnote 5 on the expenditure table: transfers to the GST compensation fund phased out from 2026-27]

claim: The Compensation Act amendment of 2018 added section 10(3A): 50% of any unspent amount the Council recommends from the Fund may be moved to the Consolidated Fund of India as the Centre's share and 50% shared among States in the ratio of their base-year revenue
source: The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Amendment Act, 2018 (No. 34 of 2018), Gazette 30 Aug 2018 (copy on gstcouncil.gov.in)
note: Why it matters: it lets the Council move unspent Fund money to the Centre and States before the transition period ends.

claim: Before COVID the Fund ran short: in 2019-20 compensation released provisionally was Rs 1,65,302 crore while cess collected was Rs 95,444 crore; cess collected was Rs 62,612 crore in 2017-18 and Rs 95,081 crore in 2018-19
source: Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance: 'GST Compensation Options' paper, annexed to PIB release of 29 Aug 2020
note: The table in the same annex gives a different 'compensation released' figure for 2019-20 (Rs 1,20,498 crore till Nov 2019) because it is a part-year; use the paragraph figure.

claim: At the 41st GST Council meeting (27 Aug 2020), the projected shortfall for 2020-21 was about Rs 3 lakh crore; on the Attorney General's opinion the States are entitled to compensation whatever the cause of the shortfall, but compensation is payable only from the Compensation Fund, the Centre is not bound to make good any shortfall, and it is for the Council to decide how
value: shortfall about Rs 3 lakh crore; AG opinion
source: Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance: 'GST Compensation Options' paper, annexed to PIB release of 29 Aug 2020
second_source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Borrowing of money to meet GST revenue shortfall' (Rajya Sabha written reply), 20 Sep 2020 [Opening paragraph: issue discussed in 41st Council meeting in light of the Attorney General's opinion]
note: The AG's opinion itself was not read; this is the Department of Expenditure's account of it.

claim: Option 1 offered to States: borrow the shortfall due to GST implementation (about Rs 97,000 crore) through a Special Window run by the Finance Ministry; the Centre would try to keep cost near the G-sec yield and bear up to 0.5% of any gap; interest paid from cess, and principal and interest after the transition period from cess by extending the cess; this borrowing not counted as State debt for Finance Commission norms
source: Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance: 'GST Compensation Options' paper, annexed to PIB release of 29 Aug 2020
second_source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Borrowing of money to meet GST revenue shortfall' (Rajya Sabha written reply), 20 Sep 2020 [Option 1 description (Rajya Sabha reply, 20 Sep 2020)]

claim: Option 2 offered to States: borrow the entire shortfall of Rs 2,35,000 crore, including the COVID part, as market debt; the Centre would commit to repay the principal from cess proceeds, but interest would be paid by the States from their own resources
value: Option 2: Rs 2,35,000 crore, States pay interest
source: Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance: 'GST Compensation Options' paper, annexed to PIB release of 29 Aug 2020
page_or_section: Option 2, items I-II and closing paragraph
second_source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Borrowing of money to meet GST revenue shortfall' (Rajya Sabha written reply), 20 Sep 2020 [Option 2]

claim: In practice the Centre borrowed from the market itself and passed the money on as back-to-back loans to the States: Rs 1.1 lakh crore for 2020-21 and Rs 1.59 lakh crore for 2021-22; the Receipt Budget puts the total at Rs 2,69,208 crore (Rs 1,10,208 crore + Rs 1,59,000 crore)
source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Payment of GST compensation to States in times of COVID-19 pandemic' (Rajya Sabha written reply), 7 Dec 2021
second_source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Receipt Budget 2026-2027, Feb 2026 [Table of borrowings, row 1.01(c), and loans table 'Back to Back Loans to State and UTs']
note: Rs 1,10,208 + 1,59,000 = 2,69,208 is our arithmetic and matches the loans table.

claim: The back-to-back loans are repaid from the Compensation Fund: Rs 78,104 crore was recovered in 2023-24, Rs 1,23,604 crore in 2024-25, and the remaining Rs 67,500 crore was to be recovered in 2025-26 (these add to Rs 2,69,208 crore, our arithmetic)
source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Receipt Budget 2026-2027, Feb 2026
page_or_section: Borrowings text, PDF p.23 (printed p.17); Statement of Assets, PDF p.63 (printed p.57)
note: Whether the 2025-26 recovery was completed is not stated in the Receipt Budget; Revised Estimates only. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Cite corrected and strengthened: repayment amounts (Rs 78,104 crore in 2023-24; Rs 1,23,604 crore in 2024-25; Rs 67,500 crore in 2025-26) are in the borrowings text of the Receipt Budget (PDF p.23, printed p.17), which labels them 'RE 2024-25' and 'BE 2025-26' (stale labels in a 2026-27 document). The Statement of Assets (PDF p.63, printed p.57) shows the back-to-back loan balance Rs 269,208 crore (end 2021-22 and 2022-23), 191,104 (2023-24), 67,500 (2024-25), then nil at end 2025-26 (RE) and 2026-27 (BE): the estimates assume full recovery by end 2025-26; actual not stated.

claim: The Centre committed in Parliament to extend the cess beyond five years to meet the shortfall and to service the loans; the Period of Levy and Collection of Cess Rules, 2022 (in force 1 Jul 2022) fixed the cess period up to 31 March 2026
source: CBIC, Goods and Services Tax (Period of Levy and Collection of Cess) Rules, 2022, issued 24 Jun 2022
second_source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Payment of GST compensation to States in times of COVID-19 pandemic' (Rajya Sabha written reply), 7 Dec 2021 [Reply: 'extending the levy of Compensation cess beyond 5 years']

claim: The States were to be compensated for five years, i.e. up to 30 June 2022, and the Government held that it was committed to compensation 'for 5 years as per the Constitutional provision'; that compensation period ended while the cess levy continued to repay loans
source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Payment of GST compensation to States in times of COVID-19 pandemic' (Rajya Sabha written reply), 7 Dec 2021
note: The end date 30 Jun 2022 is our arithmetic (1 Jul 2017 + five years); the reply states the five-year rule. No official statement of the end date was read.

claim: In Sept 2025 the Council kept the old GST rates and compensation cess on pan masala, gutkha, cigarettes, chewing tobacco, unmanufactured tobacco and bidi until the compensation-cess loan and interest obligations were fully discharged; notifications of 31 Dec 2025 then set the compensation cess on these goods to Nil from 1 February 2026

[Audit 11 Nov 2026] Both notifications confirmed in the Council's December 2025 newsletter: 19/2025-Central Tax (Rate), 31.12.2025 (rates; bidi 9%+9%, pan masala and tobacco 20%+20%) and 03/2025-Compensation Cess (Rate), 31.12.2025 (cess Nil), both from 1 Feb 2026; the newsletter's Central Tax 19/2025 and 20/2025 (RSP valuation) are different notifications. The Receipt Budget asset statement shows the back-to-back loan balance nil at end 2025-26 (RE), but no source says the loans were actually repaid. Say 'cess withdrawn from 1 Feb 2026'.

claim: The Budget 2026-27 receipts carry a separate Health Security se National Security Cess (Act of 2025) on pan masala and other goods the Centre notifies, with Rs 2,330 crore (RE 2025-26) and Rs 14,000 crore (BE 2026-27)
source: Ministry of Finance, Budget Division: Receipt Budget 2026-2027, Feb 2026

source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council held at New Delhi, today', 3 Sep 2025 (copy on gstcouncil.gov.in)

claim: The 57th GST Council meeting (8 Oct 2026) dealt with process reforms (registration, returns, refunds, adjudication), clarifications, and compliance relief; the Ministry says rate rationalisation was the work of the 56th meeting. It recommended cutting the maximum general penalty from Rs 25,000 to Rs 10,000 and raising the prosecution threshold from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore

source: PIB, Ministry of Finance: 'Recommendations of the 57th Meeting of the GST Council', 8 Oct 2026 (copy on gstcouncil.gov.in)

[Audit 11 Nov 2026] Value corrected: the 57th release also has a few item-level rate steps (psyllium seeds Nil; 5% option on EV passenger transport and rental; 5% without ITC on delivery services; TDS 2% on specified waste/scrap), so 'no rate cut' was too strong. claim: The Constitution splits the power: Union List entry 82 is 'taxes on income other than agricultural income'; State List entry 46 is 'taxes on agricultural income'
value: Union: non-agri income; State: agri income
source: Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, Lists I and II (Legislative Department file at cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in)
page_or_section: List I entry 82; List II entry 46
second_source: Constitution of India, as on 1 May 2024 (Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice; file hosted at cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in) [Article 270 and Seventh Schedule (same entries)]
note: So the Centre cannot tax agricultural income; only a State can.

claim: The Income-tax Act, 2025 (in force from 1 April 2026, replacing the 1961 Act) defines agricultural income as: rent or revenue from land in India used for agricultural purposes; income from such land by agriculture, by a cultivator's process to make the produce fit for market, or by selling produce raised; income from certain farm buildings; and income from saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery
